name: Panspermia
statement: Life may be spread between worlds, so life on Earth could have arrived from space rather than started here.
meaning: Panspermia is the hypothesis that life exists throughout the universe and is distributed between celestial bodies by cosmic dust, meteoroids, asteroids, comets, and possibly spacecraft, so that life on Earth may have arrived as a seed from elsewhere rather than arising locally. Its most important conceptual point is that panspermia addresses the transport and distribution of life, not the ultimate origin of life. Even if true, it does not explain how life first arose; it relocates that question to another world, which is both its appeal and its central limitation.
mechanism: For life to be seeded across space, it must survive ejection from one body, transit through the radiation and vacuum of space, and entry into another world's atmosphere. Rock offers the crucial shielding, which is why transfer inside meteorites, lithopanspermia, is the most credible transport route, while unshielded single spores driven by radiation pressure are quickly destroyed by ultraviolet light and cosmic rays. A well-supported weaker form, pseudo-panspermia, holds that only organic precursor molecules, not living organisms, are made in space and delivered to planets, where ordinary abiogenesis then proceeds locally.

examples.text: The Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969, is rich in organic compounds including dozens of amino acids in both handednesses, strong evidence for pseudo-panspermia, the delivery of life's building blocks.

Dried tardigrades exposed to open space on a 2007 mission survived vacuum and radiation and later bred, and radiation-resistant Deinococcus bacteria survived years outside the space station, showing organisms can endure space when shielded.
Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel speculated in 1973 that life might have been deliberately sent to Earth by an extraterrestrial intelligence, a provocative but effectively unfalsifiable variant.

variants.name: Lithopanspermia and pseudo-panspermia
variants.text: Transfer of life inside rock, the most respectable transport form, versus the well-supported delivery of only organic precursor molecules, which feeds ordinary abiogenesis rather than seeding life itself.

variants.name: Radiopanspermia and directed panspermia
variants.text: Arrhenius's radiation-pressure transport of spores, now considered implausible unshielded, and Crick and Orgel's deliberate seeding by an intelligence, regarded as unfalsifiable.

whyItMatters: Panspermia bears on origin-of-life research and astrobiology: it reframes where and how first life might have begun, and its well-supported pseudo-panspermia form directly informs prebiotic chemistry by supplying an established off-world source of organic building blocks. It motivates planetary-protection concerns about contaminating other worlds, and it drives testable research programmes, from meteorite organic analysis to orbital exposure experiments and sample-return missions, even in its unproven transport forms.

working.text: read panspermia as a claim about how life spreads, not how it began, since it relocates rather than answers the origin question.
treat pseudo-panspermia as well-supported, lithopanspermia as speculative but respectable, and disease-from-space claims as fringe.
note that organisms enduring space conditions shows survivability, not the full ejection, transit, and arrival a real seeding requires.

limits: Its defining limitation is that it does not solve the origin of life; it relocates abiogenesis to another body, and pseudo-panspermia is compatible with ordinary abiogenesis on Earth. Radiation and transit hazards make unshielded single-spore transport implausible over long distances. The strong claims of Fred Hoyle and Chandra Wickramasinghe, in particular that terrestrial epidemics are seeded from comets, are rejected by the mainstream, and directed panspermia is effectively unfalsifiable. Credibility divides sharply by tier: pseudo-panspermia is well-supported, lithopanspermia speculative but respectable, radiopanspermia largely superseded, and the disease-from-space claims fringe.
misreadings: It does not explain how life originated; it only addresses transport and moves the origin question elsewhere. Organic molecules in meteorites support pseudo-panspermia, the delivery of building blocks, not the arrival of living organisms. Tardigrades or bacteria surviving in orbit prove limited survivability under shielding, not the complete interplanetary journey. Not all forms are fringe: pseudo-panspermia is mainstream-supported, and only the strongest claims are rejected. And directed panspermia, deliberate seeding by an intelligence, is one specific speculative sub-variant, not panspermia as a whole.
origin: An idea traced to the ancient Greek Anaxagoras, revived in the nineteenth century by Lord Kelvin and Hermann von Helmholtz, cast as a scientific hypothesis by Svante Arrhenius in the early 1900s, and given a directed form by Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel in 1973.
